# Ekakanipāta (AN 1)

**ID:** AN 1
**Section:** Aṅguttaranikāya (an)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Ekakanipāta

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ekakanipāta* ("The Book of the Ones") constitutes the first major collection of the *Aṅguttaranikāya*, organizing teachings and doctrinal items into a single numerical classification [Bodhi 1970]. Across its various chapters, it presents short discourses centered on singular phenomena, ranging from the dangers of improper attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*) and unwholesome mental roots [Bodhi 1970] to the practice of mindfulness as a receptive middle path avoiding self-mortification and sense indulgence [Nauriyal 2006]. The nipāta famously includes passages affirming that the mind is fundamentally luminous (*pabhassara*) but corrupted by adventitious (*āgantuka*) defilements (AN 1.5–6, 1.10, and the "finger-snap" passages of AN 1.12ff), a doctrine that exerted long-standing influence across early Buddhist and later Mahāyāna thought [Almogi 2014; Nauriyal 2006; Powers 2016]. A major section is the *Etadaggavagga* (AN 1, chapter 14), in which the Buddha identifies eighty categories of foremost disciples, establishing the preeminence of figures such as Mahākassapa in ascetic (*dhuta*) practices, Anuruddha in concentration, Ānanda in personal attendance, and Bhaddā Kapilānī in the recollection of past lives [Nauriyal 2006; Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003; Silk 1994]. In the commentary, the *Manorathapūraṇī* on the *Ekakanipāta* (*Ekakanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*) preserves influential accounts regarding the gradual decline and disappearance of the Buddha's dispensation (*sāsana*) [Turner 2009].

 DharmaNexus identifies extensive Pali-internal text reuse with collections such as the *Sacca Saṁyutta* (SN 56), the *Bojjhaṅga Saṁyutta* (SN 46), the *Ñāṇavibhaṅga* (Vb 16), the *Bahudhātuka Sutta* (MN 115), and other nipātas of the *Aṅguttaranikāya* [DharmaNexus]. Furthermore, DharmaNexus generates cross-language alignments with Sanskrit fragments of the *Ekottarāgama*, Mahāyāna sūtras including the *Daśasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, and scholastic treatises such as the *Śrāvakabhūmi* and Candrakīrti's *Madhyamakāvatāra* [DharmaNexus].
